newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rain disrupts maize harvest in southwest France.
newsitem.headline: Rain disrupts maize harvest in southwest France.

text.p: Rain is holding up combining of early variety maize in France's southwest and threatening to seriously push back the start of the bulk of the harvest, crop analysts said on Friday.
In the Aquitaine region, the country's top maize producer, first cuttings of maize started in early September but rain forced farmers to abandon their fields this week.
"Scattered rains made it useless to get into the fields one day and stop working the next day," one analyst for the local ONIC grain office in Bordeaux told Reuters.
The bulk of the harvest normally starts in early October in the region but analysts now predict delays of up to two weeks.

Local ONIC officials said they were not too concerned over possible quality or yield loss for the the main crop at this stage, sticking to their previous forecast of a local yield of 8.6 tonnes per hectare against 8.0 tonnes last year.
But the main fear was that high humidity might rot roots and winds could tip over plants, they said.
Because producers are under pressure to get freshly cut maize to ports as rapidly as possible, some farmers have not given their crops enough time to fully mature.
Early results from cuttings of early variety maize thus show disappointing yields, analysts said.
Prompt delivery maize prices firmed this week as operators worried about meeting their commitments to deliver to ports, dealers said.
In the Midi-Pyrenees region, ONIC officials said they were not concerned over possible delays as the bulk of the harvest traditionally starts in mid-October.
But rain was preventing farmers from completing the sunflower harvest, they said.
In eastern France, the first cuttings of early variety maize began last week but progress had been slow because cool temperatures did not allow the grain to fully mature.
But dry weather should help the harvest start as scheduled next week.
Local yields are seen jumping to 9.5 tonnes this year from 8.9 tonnes and area to 126,000 hectares from 115,000 ha.
The French maize growers' association, AGPM, expects the national crop to jump by one million tonnes to 13.8 million in 1996.
